abstract: Quantitative detection of radical-associated magnetic activity in living cells remains challenging because variations between quantum sensors complicate direct comparisons of intracellular environments. Here, we demonstrate a label-free quantum sensing platform based on substrate-fixed diamond nanopillars containing individually addressable nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. The fixed architecture enables one-to-one measurements using identical NV sensors in the presence and absence of cells, minimizing sensor-to-sensor variability and allowing reliable assessment of cellular contributions to spin decoherence. Cellular compatibility assays supported preserved metabolic activity, DNA synthesis, and membrane integrity without detectable apoptotic activation. Intracellular NV centers retained approximately 10% optically detected magnetic resonance contrast, 20% Rabi contrast, and a Hahn-echo coherence time T2 of approximately 3 {micro}s. Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill dynamical decoupling extended intracellular T2 to 25.8 {+/-} 4.90 {micro}s. We applied this platform to embryonic stem (ES) cells undergoing doxycycline-induced differentiation toward the trophectoderm lineage. Identical NV sensors exhibited consistent coherence recovery following removal of differentiation-induced cells, whereas undifferentiated controls showed no systematic recovery. Calibration using the stable radical TEMPOL, supported by magnetic-noise modeling and kinetic Monte Carlo simulations, enabled numerical evaluation of local magnetic responses as model-dependent TEMPOL-equivalent spin densities of 0.084-0.567 spins/nm3 across different sensing sites. These findings establish a quantitative approach to investigating intracellular physicochemical changes during stem-cell differentiation and demonstrate the potential of quantum sensing to study biological processes relevant to tissue development and regenerative medicine.
